The Dewey Crew on the Kassel Mission

On the morning of 27 September 1944, 2nd Lt. William R. Dewey lifted his B-24J off the runway at Tibenham for his eighth combat mission. His aircraft was number 855, nicknamed A-Abel — the ‘A’ ship of the 701st Squadron. The target was the Henschel works at Kassel. Forty planes were dispatched in four ten-ship squadrons; three aborted. Dewey flew left wing of the lead element of the high-high-right squadron, and could not have known the day would become the worst single-mission loss any group suffered in the war.

After bombs-away the group turned for England, and the Luftwaffe’s Sturmgruppen fell on them. Dewey’s tail gunner, Ruben “Monty” Montanez, called it first.

“I see fighters, I see flak.” Then the entire plane began to shudder and shake, with the guns in the rear firing simultaneously and from the impact of 20mm and 30mm enemy shells. — William R. Dewey, “Divine Providence,” 8th AF News, 1989

The intercom to the rear was severed within seconds; top-turret gunner Charley Craig reported five fighters on their tail. Then, in “maybe three to five minutes,” it was over. Only seven Liberators were left to form on the surviving pathfinder ship. More fighters at eleven o’clock low proved friendly — P-51s of the 361st Fighter Group, sweeping in to break up the slaughter.

A-Abel was wrecked but flying: the tail turret afire, both waist gunners and the tail gunner wounded, a huge hole in the right waist, control cables partly cut, and a three-foot hole in the wing behind the No. 3 engine spilling 100-octane fuel into the slipstream. With the waist out of oxygen, navigator Herb Bailey took over the nose turret while nose gunner Les Medlock made trip after trip through the bomb bay carrying oxygen bottles to the wounded, covering them with his jacket and giving first aid.

Rather than risk ditching in the Channel, Dewey chose to nurse the ship to the nearest field to get his wounded to a hospital faster. He called air-sea rescue — “Colgate” — which fixed his position and gave him a heading, while an enemy 109 trailed below for minutes waiting for them to fall. About an hour later they broke through the cloud to the white cliffs of Dover and the long runways of RAF Manston.

“The landing gear went down and locked perfectly, the flaps went down all the way and the tires were fully inflated. The landing was one of the best I ever made in a B-24 — like we were on feathers. A day we will never forget — 27 September 1944!” — William R. Dewey

Decades later, William Dewey founded the Kassel Mission Memorial Association, gathering combat reports, German records and survivor accounts — American and German alike — into The Kassel Mission Reports and the Kassel Mission Chronicles, and helping dedicate the 1990 memorial near Bad Hersfeld. “None of us bear any animosity,” he told schoolchildren that year. “We were doing our duty as soldiers, and they were protecting their country.”

Sources: William R. Dewey, “Divine Providence” and “Disaster at Kassel”; gunners’ combat narratives (Montanez, Johnson, Bartkow); KM Chronicles (1998). KMHS archive.

The Bruland Crew — B-24H “Texas Rose,” 701st Squadron

On the morning of 27 September 1944, 2nd Lt. Palmer M. Bruland climbed into a B-24H Liberator he barely knew, with a crew he had never met. His ship was Texas Rose, serial 41-28922, of the 701st Squadron, flying out of Tibenham against the marshalling yards at Kassel. Bruland and his co-pilot, 2nd Lt. Peter S. Belitsos, had been thrown together with a borrowed crew only hours before takeoff. As Belitsos later wrote, he was tapped on the shoulder before dawn and told he was flying with Bruland’s crew: “I was taken to the hardstand where I met Palmer Bruland for the first time. I introduced myself… This took place before dawn and I did not meet the rest of the crew or see them face to face except for the engineer.”

The Kassel Mission became the costliest single-group air battle of the Eighth Air Force. When German fighters fell on the 445th, they struck with annihilating speed. Belitsos remembered no warning at all: “The first sign for me was a thud that shook the plane and then the inboard engine on my side caught fire. Simultaneously I saw that almost all of the planes in my line of vision were on fire.” Bruland took over the controls as Belitsos worked the feathering procedure with the engineer; the fire would not go out. They nursed Texas Rose down from 20,000 feet, hoping to reach France, but at last the order came to bail out. “Everyone cleared the plane,” Belitsos wrote. “Bruland was the last man out.”

All nine men aboard parachuted alive. The German crash report (MACR 9386) records the Liberator going down near Gießen at about 11:25, “durch Jäger beim Rückflug” — by fighters on the return flight. Yet survival in the air did not mean safety on the ground. Two of the gunners reassigned to this scratch crew that very morning — nose-turret gunner S/Sgt. Ferdinand K. Flach and waist gunner S/Sgt. Lee R. J. Huffman — came down by parachute, were taken prisoner, and were then murdered by German military personnel. The crash sheet marks both men with the single German word tot — dead — while their seven crewmates are listed as POW.

The killings became a United States war-crimes case, tried at Dachau in 1946 (Case No. 12-472, United States v. Hermann Noack and Karl Georg Boess). The court found that two captured, unarmed American airmen were driven from the village of Hattenrod under guard, marched into the fields, and shot. A witness testified that as one body lay in an open field, Hauptmann Hermann Noack — a former Luftwaffe paratrooper who ran a local Hitler Youth camp — was reported to have said, “Revenge for the first sergeant.” Each man had been shot under the pretense of “attempting to escape.” Noack was sentenced to death by hanging; his driver, the butcher Karl Georg Boess — whose own teenage son had been killed when his train was strafed by Allied planes shortly before — received eight years.

The Society’s archive preserves the long aftermath. A memoir by an American officer who served at Landsberg War Crimes Prison records that Noack escaped one stormy night by a knotted bedsheet rope, was recaptured and shot in the leg (later amputated), attempted suicide, and was finally hanged on 21 March 1947. Asked for his last words, “Noack mumbled barely audible words saying he was not angry at the two pilots.” Lee Huffman rests today beneath a grave marker at the Netherlands American Cemetery, Margraten. He and Flach were on Bruland’s plane for one mission, strangers to the men beside them, and they did not come home.

Sources: Peter Belitsos, “Fill-In Co-Pilot,” The Kassel Mission Reports, Addendum 1994; German US Aircraft Crash Data sheet, MACR 9386; Bruland crew photograph and roster; Review and Recommendations, United States v. Hermann Noack and Karl Georg Boess, Case No. 12-472 (1946); Tom Atkinson, “Captor & Captive” (Girtman Press); Lee Huffman grave-marker photograph, Margraten, courtesy Jean Vankan. KMHS archive.

The Uebelhoer Crew — Deputy Lead of the 445th

On the morning of 27 September 1944, Capt. Web L. Uebelhoer of the 700th Bomb Squadron lifted his B-24J off the runway at Tibenham not as a wingman but as the deputy lead of the entire 445th Bomb Group — the second-in-command ship, carrying deputy mission commander Capt. James Graham in the right seat. It was Uebelhoer’s 18th mission, and by his own reckoning “mentally, it was an average mission.” It would become anything but.

A combat veteran who had crossed with the 492nd Bomb Group and belly-landed out of fuel on his very first sortie (“that’s the way I started out in combat”), Uebelhoer understood the iron discipline of the deputy slot. As his navigator, 1st Lt. Don Whitefield, put it: “We were deputy lead, and when you’re deputy lead, you do what lead plane does…. If he’s wrong, we have to follow right with that lead.” That obedience is the heart of the tragedy. Battling a 75-mph headwind — “we were up there in a damn hurricane,” Whitefield recalled — the lead ship turned left off course past the Initial Point. Through 100 percent cloud, the formation drifted, then bombed not Kassel but the vicinity of Göttingen. Over interphone Uebelhoer heard his crew’s alarm: “Hey! We’re drifting away from the main stream!” But with command pilot Graham aboard, he kept silent on the radio — “I was flying the aircraft, and I was talking to my crew.”

When the formation turned for the reassembly point, the cost of the error became plain: “we looked out, and we were thirty-some airplanes all alone. And the fighter planes did not see us go.” Then tail gunner John Hubicz called: “Captain, there’s a hell of a lot of aircraft behind us!” Uebelhoer assumed they were friendly — until the cannon bursts began to spot the sky. More than 100 Luftwaffe fighters fell on the isolated 445th. Flying perhaps 50 feet off the lead ship, Uebelhoer watched Maj. Donald McCoy in the right-seat window “signaling me but I didn’t know what” — an image Whitefield independently confirmed. An FW-190 stood on its tail, the lead ship glowed “an orange appearance,” and Chilton’s aircraft rolled left and went down. “Now in the meantime,” Uebelhoer said simply, “the lead ship’s shot down so I’m the leader.”

He took the formation. His nose gunner sprayed the armored Germans “like a garden hose”; he got on the interphone and chewed out his own crew — “Hey, let’s get in this fight!” — until “every weapon on that ship was firing.” Then four P-38s swept overhead and “we realized the cavalry had arrived.” Uebelhoer brought his ship home to Tibenham — one of only a handful to return — with a single projectile through the No. 2 engine’s self-sealing oil reservoir. Taxiing in, he only learned the truth when “somebody later said, ‘Hey, you got shot.’”

That night, amid a confused debriefing, even Jimmy Stewart drove to the base and stood on the edge of the crowd, listening — “I think that he almost became ill listening to what had happened.” Days later the 445th went back to Kassel, and “those fighter pilots made damn sure that they protected us this time.” When Col. Jones later offered Uebelhoer a squadron command — a promotion that meant returning to combat — he weighed it and answered, “Thanks but no thanks.”

Sources: Web Uebelhoer interview by Aaron Elson, Savannah, GA, 30 Sept. 1999; Don Whitefield, recollections to Linda Dewey, 27 July 2007 and 26 Feb. 2008; KMHS crew photo and roster (courtesy Web Uebelhoer). KMHS archive.

The Pearson Crew on the Kassel Mission

On 27 September 1944, 1st Lt. Ralph H. Pearson of Falconer, New York, took B-24J Liberator 44-10497 off the runway at Tibenham with the 700th Squadron. It was his 29th mission, and the first 28 had been almost routine — “We didn’t even blow a tire,” he told the Jamestown Post-Journal. “On the 29th mission, however, that was a different story.”

After a navigational error carried the 445th off its briefed track and away from its fighter escort, an estimated 100–200 Focke-Wulf 190s and Messerschmitt 109s fell on the unprotected formation near Eisenach. “The Storm would fly into battle 15 abreast to force the formation to scatter,” Pearson recalled. Flying the vulnerable low slot, his ship was among the first hit; radio operator Doye O’Keefe believed they “were probably the first plane shot down.”

The first shell exploded in the nose, killing navigator 2nd Lt. Arthur Stearns and bombardier F/O Henry Henrikson at their stations. A second started a gasoline fire between the bomb bay and the nose; O’Keefe fought it but found burning aviation fuel almost impossible to put out. With the cockpit ablaze and the control cables finally burning through, Pearson ordered the crew out.

“When the chute opened, it jerked me so hard that my beautiful fleece-lined flight boots came off. As I floated down in my stocking feet I thought, ‘Nuts, some German kid is going to be wearing those comfortable boots.’” — 1st Lt. Ralph Pearson, “Shot Down on the Kassel Raid”

Pearson clawed back through the fire to the bomb bay — searing off his eyebrows and badly burning his face — waved engineer Robert Johnson out ahead of him, and jumped from about 25,000 feet. The German fighters circled his parachute; he played dead, and they only radioed his position. He came down near Herleshausen, about 200 meters south of the Siegelshof, and was driven by motorcycle sidecar to a Luftwaffe hospital, his face bandaged “like a mummy.” He spent eight months as a prisoner at Stalag Luft I; his German interrogation folder, he later learned, bore a single word — kräftig, “strong soldier.”

Of the 35 crews over the target, only four planes returned to Tibenham. The Pearson crew lost three men killed — navigator Stearns, bombardier Henrikson, and top-turret gunner T/Sgt. Robert D. Johnson; the rest survived as prisoners of war.

Sources: Ralph Pearson, “Shot Down on the Kassel Raid” (in A Hometown Went to War); Doye O’Keefe oral history (1985); Harry Tachovsky in The Morning Call (1995); German crash-data form, MACR 9384. KMHS archive.

The Hunter Crew — B-24H “Terrible Terry’s Terror”

On 27 September 1944, the B-24H Liberator Terrible Terry’s Terror (serial 42-94810) flew the left-wing slot of the lead element of the 700th Bomb Squadron, 445th Bomb Group, on the mission that would become known as the Kassel disaster. At the controls was 1st Lt. William F. Hunter of Essex Junction, Vermont. The ship had been named for the group’s first commander, Col. Robert H. Terrill — a nose-art tribute that the crew would soon make legendary in its own right.

Riding along that day was a photo observer, S/Sgt. Thomas G. Spera of Philadelphia, whose account survives in the Society’s archive and remains the most vivid record of what the crew endured. Spera recalled that the run began deceptively: “Up until that time, I had chalked up the mission as a ‘milk run.’” Then, after the bombs were away, more than 200 Luftwaffe fighters fell on the under-escorted formation. “In less time than it takes to tell, the sky was full of debris from exploding ships,” he wrote. “The leading Liberator, on fire from nose to tail, came swinging toward us like a severely wounded animal, then peeled away as if to pick a spot away from us to die.”

Then Terrible Terry’s Terror was hit. “A 20-millimeter shell tore through the bomb bay, ripping off the doors and severing fuel lines. Two fires started simultaneously in the bay.” What followed was the act that defined the crew. The engineer, T/Sgt. Robert N. Ratchford of Gastonia, North Carolina, “threw off his parachute, grabbed a fire extinguisher, and put both fires out before the 100-octane gas had been ignited,” then plugged the leaks while “fuel was pouring out like water from a fire hydrant.” Gasoline soaked the three men in the waist; a bubble of it pooled on the camera hatch. The Society’s crew file records the verdict plainly: the men “were lucky there was no fire, as the bomb bay and waist had been awash with leaking gas. The engineer, Ratchford, did a heroic job in plugging these leaks even though he was soaked in fuel.”

The gunners gave as good as they got. Spera watched a Focke-Wulf “hang by his propeller only a few yards off our left wing” before it was “riddled by fire from our top turret guns,” manned by Sgt. Robert W. Sarber; the interrogating officer’s report notes the enemy fighter “virtually blew up.” Tail gunner S/Sgt. Fred C. Schaffer, Jr. sent another down in flames, and right-waist gunner S/Sgt. Joseph K. Selser claimed a probable. A bullet through the waist proved a strange mercy: Spera’s oxygen line had pulled loose and he was blacking out until the round prompted a gunner to look around, see his trouble, and reconnect the line.

Six minutes later the attacks ended as abruptly as they had begun — of four squadrons, Spera could count only ten surviving ships. With one engine gone and a second quitting on approach, Hunter limped the crippled bomber toward newly liberated France, an escort of P-51 Mustangs answering the radioman’s call. He “cleared a clump of trees by inches, clipped a set of high tension wires, and brought the ship down on a potato patch” near the village of Willems, east of Lille. The only injury was a cut hand; the aircraft was a total loss. Villagers “stopped at nothing to make us comfortable,” Spera wrote, and the crew left for an RAF base “still marveling to find ourselves alive.”

Lt. Hunter received the Distinguished Flying Cross for his airmanship that day. The story does not end happily. The men became a lead crew and transferred to the 389th Bomb Group; on 9 March 1945, over Munster, their Liberator took a direct flak burst in the wing fuel tanks and went down in flames. Only Schaffer and a recently assigned radar officer escaped, both badly burned and taken prisoner. Hunter and most of his Kassel crew were killed and are buried at Margraten, Holland. Spera, who had moved on before that final flight, survived the war.

Sources: S/Sgt. Thomas G. Spera, eyewitness account (via Mary Beth Barnard, 445th BG historian; submitted by George M. Collar, 1990); 445th BG crew-data forms and annotated crew photographs (George Collar); 700th BS combat encounter reports of Schaffer, Selser, and Sarber (27 Sept 1944); Missing Air Crew roster, Munster raid, 9 Mar 1945; “Blaze of Glory” newspaper clipping. KMHS archive.

1st Lt. Raymond V. Heitz Crew — B-24H “Bugs Bunny,” 700th Squadron

On 27 September 1944 the crew of 1st Lt. Raymond V. Heitz flew B-24H Liberator #42-95210, “Bugs Bunny,” on the 445th Bomb Group’s strike toward Kassel. It was, by the reckoning of the ship’s radio operator, a milestone sortie. “I was radio operator on Lt. Heitz’s crew and we were on our 23rd mission,” Fabian Mack wrote in a 1990 letter preserved in the Society’s files. What began as a routine count toward the end of a combat tour became one of the most violent few minutes any of them would know.

When the Luftwaffe’s massed fighters fell on the unescorted 445th, the gunners of “Bugs Bunny” met them head-on. Tail gunner S/Sgt. Maynard B. Watson left an account of extraordinary intensity. As eleven FW-190s dived and three turned in on his ship, he opened fire at long range: “The center one was exactly 6 o’clock. He came into my fire to about 600 yards and blew up all at once, into about 4 pieces and a million smaller ones.” A second fighter followed — “the pilot pops out and the plane starts into a dive and bursts into flames” — then a third, which “stalled in the air and started down, then exploded, almost in my face.”

Then the bomber itself was hit. “All hell broke loose,” Watson wrote. “I was hit in the back and several shells exploded under my feet. I was blown out of the turret.” A news clipping in the archive records that cannon fire “destroyed the oxygen and hydraulic systems, cut the interphone connections, pierced fuel tanks, and set fire to five emergency dinghies stored in the waist.” Waist gunner S/Sgt. Louis Ochevsky was killed and S/Sgt. Elroy Palm wounded; Watson, recovering consciousness, smothered the fire in the tail, took over the unmanned waist gun, and with Palm jettisoned the smoldering dinghies, “averting an otherwise fatal explosion from the igniting gas fumes.”

“We lost two engines during the attack … with three badly wounded aboard we got our gear down and with the aid of two chutes set her down in a field about 15 miles East of Brussels.” — T/Sgt. Fabian Mack, radio operator

Flight engineer T/Sgt. Homer Harrison had already shown his nerve: when the bomb-bay doors jammed open, his wife Christine recalled, he “walked the broken bomb bay doors” without a parachute and kicked them shut. He bailed out just before the rough landing, reasoning “it would be better to roll out rather than blow up.” On the ground in liberated Belgium, Mack got the casualties to a British field hospital with the help of Belgian civilians: “One passed away that evening, the other two recovered and came back to finish their tour.”

Louis Ochevsky was awarded the Silver Star and credited with a fighter destroyed — posthumously; Palm and Watson each received the Silver Star as well. Years later, the bonds outlasted the war: Harrison spotted co-pilot Harold Vedera on a Sacramento street, and found Palm — by then an English policeman — on a street in England. “We went merrily along,” Watson had written of the moment the sky cleared over Belgium, “as happy as if we all had good sense.”

Sources: Fabian Mack letter (9 Jan 1990); Maynard Watson’s account and combat claim forms (27 Sept 1944); “2 Lib Gunners Silver Starred” clipping; interview with Christine Harrison; Heitz crew roster; 2nd ADA Journal (Winter 1989). KMHS archive.

The Hansen Crew — B-24H #42-95078, 700th Squadron

At 0215 on 27 September 1944, the charge of quarters woke the crew of 2nd Lt. Robert N. “Pappy” Hansen with word that briefing was at 0500. When the curtain came back from the map, the target was Kassel — deep enough to matter, but, as bombardier 2nd Lt. John C. “Woody” Woodley recalled, it “while far from being a ‘milk run,’ wasn’t too far into Germany, and we stood a good chance of getting back early for chow.” Their own ship, “fondly christened ‘Patches,’” had been marked off the board, so the men drew a reserve B-24H, #42-95078, and lifted off from Tibenham into a routine assembly over a 10/10ths undercast.

As the 445th turned off the target it drifted from the bomber stream and was left alone. Woodley remembered the false calm: “About 1000 we were all feeling good, and Pappy Hansen, our pilot, and I were talking about how lucky we were to have gotten a milk run.” Then the gunners called out fighters — co-pilot Herbert Bridges later estimated “approximately 150 FW 190’s.”

“20 MM shells were breaking in front, looking exactly like small flak bursts. They were pumping explosives into our midsection, and I saw several ships fall away, either exploding or burning fiercely… At this time I noticed that our left wing tip had been carried away.” — 2nd Lt. John C. Woodley, diary

Woodley fired until his turret guns went dead, then found “the midsection of the ship was blazing, and the fire extended as far forward as the rear of the nose wheel doors.” He crawled to the nose-wheel hatch: “About this time the ship gave a lurch, and out and away I fell.” The clearest record of the final moments comes from co-pilot Bridges, who in July 1945 wrote the War Department a careful account: the navigator, Porter Pile, wounded in the leg, “would not jump when told by bombardier”; waist gunner S. E. Howell, shot in the chest, was pushed out the rear hatch; tail gunner Ralph Bode stood ready to follow.

“Pilot, R. N. Hansen, was still at the controls and engineer, C. C. Palmer, and radio operator, J. M. Triplett, were standing by top escape hatch dubious about jumping. Since I was off oxygen, I went on out… right after bailing out, I looked up and could see nothing but two chutes.” — 2nd Lt. Herbert C. Bridges, casualty report, 1945

Of the nine men, only three lived. The German crash-data form (MACR 9396) records the ship going down between about 11:03 and 11:09 “Im Trottenwald (Oberschaar), 2 km südwestlich Richelsdorf,” the cause noted simply as “durch Jäger beim Rückflug” — by fighters on the return flight. Six were killed; Bridges, Woodley, and waist gunner Elwyn Hornsby were taken prisoner. Woodley’s descent read like deliverance: “Everything was very quiet and peaceful after the terrific din of engines and guns.” On the ground he helped interpret for a German woman, Margarete Scherer, who treated him and a badly burned gunner from another downed ship before they were carried off to captivity, and Stalag Luft I — where he kept the diary that preserves this story.

Sources: John C. Woodley diary and POW accounts; Herbert C. Bridges casualty report (1945); German crash-data form, MACR 9396; “Ex-POWs of Alabama” (1984). KMHS archive.

Many valuable accounts and interviews have been generously left behind by these veterans of the Kassel Mission. All are riveting. The diary of S/Sgt. Herbert R. Schwartz, below, stands out among these.

The original crew of Lt. John French. Back row, L to R: Lt. John French, pilot; Lt. Claude Switzler, bombardier; Lt. Robert Tims, navigator; Lt. Robert Cochran, copilot. Front row, L to R: Sgt. Calvin Hayward; Sgt. Moynnihan, engineer; Sgt. David Greenley; Sgt. Mitchell O'Kelly, radio operator; Sgt. Ostertag, tail gunner; Sgt. Harold Winand. Of this crew, only French, Cochran, Tims, and Greenley flew the Kassel Mission.

The French Crew on the Kassel Mission

On 27 September 1944, 1st Lt. John E. French and his crew lifted off from Tibenham in B-24J Liberator 42-50784, flying lead of the high-right element. When the lead radar operator fixed on the wrong town — Göttingen instead of Kassel — the whole group drifted off the bomber stream and out from under its escort. Navigator Robert T. Tims described the moment the trap closed:

“Suddenly, coming in at six o’clock low, wave after murderous wave, the FW-190s, over a hundred of them … firing tracers and 30 mm cannon bursts blinking like Christmas tree lights; then everywhere around us burning and exploding B-24s … the chutes gently sprouting like white mushrooms below us.” — Robert T. Tims, Carnage Over Kassel

The crew’s gunners fought back hard, and three of them were credited with destroying FW-190s. From the tail, S/Sgt Herbert Schwartz held his sights on a fighter boring straight in and set it afire at seventy-five yards; from the right waist, S/Sgt Charles Huddleston sent another down in flames; and from the left waist, S/Sgt James Corman knocked down the fighter that had shot out their No. 1 engine, then a second.

“The second plane … flew a perfect pursuit curve. I saw the pilot’s face and shot him; his fuselage caught on fire. Then the right wing fell off and the pilot pitched forward.” — S/Sgt James Corman

The Liberator was mortally hurt — a 20mm shell tore off the bomb-bay doors and started two fires over the fuel tanks. The engineer threw off his own parachute, seized an extinguisher and beat out both fires before the gasoline caught. With the No. 1 engine dead and the right rudder shot away, French nursed the shuddering bomber west on two and three engines, a lost straggler, and aimed for liberated France. Photo-observer T/Sgt Thomas Spera, riding in the waist, recorded the final seconds:

“By inches, clipped a set of high-tension wires, and brought the ship down on a potato patch … only to have one wheel catch in a hole, buckle, and dig the right wing into the ground. We all took a severe bouncing, but our only casualty was a cut hand for the bombardier.” — T/Sgt Thomas Spera

The Liberator was a total loss; all nine aboard walked away — one of only a handful of the group’s ships to escape the slaughter.

Sources: Robert T. Tims, “Carnage Over Kassel” (2nd ADA Journal, 1989); Thomas Spera account; gunners’ combat claim forms, 27 Sept 1944. KMHS archive.

The Carrow Crew — B-24J “Patches”

27 September 1944 “began as all the others had,” pilot 1st Lt. Raphael E. Carrow remembered, “being rudely awakened in the earliest hours of the morning. A thick fog reflected the sharp beam of the bicycle light as I pedalled, more intuitively than visually, to the mess hall.” His Liberator, Patches, flew the low-left element in the No. 9 position of the lead squadron — the 445th was the lead group, “the first over the North Sea, the first to cross the mainland.” It was the crew’s twenty-first mission.

Cloud forced a radar drop, and the lead ship veered off course. Carrow saw it at once. “We were supposed to keep radio silence but some of us didn’t,” he recalled. “I was one of those who didn’t. I said, ‘We’re going the wrong way!’” The order came back to stay in line. The 445th bombed Göttingen by mistake, then turned for home alone, fifty miles behind the protected main force. Near Bad Hersfeld some 150 fighters fell on them.

“All around us was fire, black smoke, planes going down, more parachutes… machine guns firing — the shudder of 20mm shells hitting — another engine gone — intercom out — plane out of control — a gripping fear-near panic — then, fire! The bomb bay was a roaring inferno.” — Raphael Carrow, Just Another Rude Awakening

Carrow touched co-pilot Newell Brainard on the arm and pointed to the fire; Brainard left his seat, and Carrow never saw him again. Then came the moment that nearly killed him: “Now I had to find a way out, but I was frozen to the seat!” Unbuckling the belt, shedding flak vest and Mae West — each “presented an alternative death.” That very paralysis saved him. By the time he wrenched free, the aircraft had torn apart: “Instead of the expected inferno, I saw blue sky. The plane had broken in two and the other half had taken the fire with it.” He shoved into space and pulled the cord inside a cloud, breaking clear barely two hundred yards above the ground, the hair burned from the back of his head.

Patches came down at Iba, about 44 miles southeast of Kassel. Carrow landed inside a fenced slave-labor camp, where an elderly guard leveled a rifle and spat one word: “Jude?” Carrow — a Brooklyn-born Jew who never wore dog tags on a mission — said nothing and was marched into the stockade. Five of the nine aboard were killed and four taken prisoner. The cruelest fate fell to Brainard: wounded in the head and first given Red Cross aid, he was taken to the labor camp at Nentershausen, interrogated, beaten, led outside and shot, then buried in a single grave. His family was told only “killed in action” — until German historian Walter Hassenpflug pieced the truth together and his sister read a burial report on which one word “could clearly be read: ‘Murdered.’”

Carrow was interrogated at Dulag Luft — where his recovered flight log had already given the Germans the crew’s names — and imprisoned at Stalag Luft I at Barth. He entered captivity near 180 pounds and left at 120, liberated by the Russians in 1945.

Sources: Raphael Carrow, “Just Another Rude Awakening” (Kassel Mission Reports Addendum, 1994) and Aaron Elson interview (1999); German crash-data form, MACR 9399; Duane Giesler KMHS narrative; Kay Brainard Hutchins, The Palm Beach Post (1992). KMHS archive.

(See that unbelievable story by clicking clicking here). The Bruce crew was one of the only crews to fly its original aircraft, the Bonnie Vee, named for Bruce's wife, Verlyn. Unfortunately, Bonnie Vee exploded in this battle, and everyone but the pilot and his radio operator were killed.

THE BONNIE VEE STORY

BOMBARDIER AND KMMA HISTORIAN GEORGE COLLAR TELLS THE BRUCE CREW STORY, AS RECORDED BY KMHS ORAL HISTORIAN AARON ELSON.

Bill Bruce was on a mission. The ship he flew was called Bonnie V, and it was named after his wife, whose name was Verlyn. And he was on about his tenth...mission, so he was still a second lieutenant when he got shot down on the Kassel raid.

But anyway, they went, I think it was in July or sometime prior to the Kassel Mission, on this bomb run and they got hit by flak in the tail, and I've got a picture of that damn thing with the tail all shot up, and he had a hell of a time getting home with it. And the co-pilot was a fellow named Brown that lives down in North Carolina, and a piece of flak practically severed his leg.

Well, you know what they did? The gunner got down, the top gunner come down and put a tourniquet on it, and it took two of them to get this plane [under control]. Everything was shot up and ready to go down, and fighting the stick was tough, see. And that guy stayed conscious and helped get that damn plane back down. And when they got him home, they took him out of there and they thought he was gonna die, he lost a lot of blood.

By God, he come out of it, and Mrs. Bruce told me over to the phone, she said, he's still alive and lives in North Carolina and he makes his own prostheses, because he didn't like the ones they had. He plays golf and everything.

What was unique about Bruce is the fact that his first co-pilot got his leg shot off, and then the second guy came, a guy by the name of Walter [correction: John] Willett who was a first lieutenant, and poor old Bruce is still a second lieutenant, and this Willett had a lot of flying time but he'd never been in combat, and somebody told him if you ever want to go up the ladder you've got to get in combat. So he had a friend at the 445th who said "Come on over." And so he joined up with the 445th, and they put him on as co-pilot, and it might have been his first—well, no, I don't know how many missions Bruce did between the time Brown got it and Willett—but Willets got shot, his head or something, got shot right off [ed. note: a rocket sheared Willett in two through the torso], sitting right next to Bruce. It's in his story.

FROM THE DIARY OF HERBERT R. SCHWARTZ, TAIL GUNNER, FRENCH CREW, WHICH FLEW JUST IN FRONT OF BONNIE VEE

Everyone started firing & before I knew it, they were in on us. 100 Fockewolfes (sic), and I was half scared to death. They were thru us and started to re-form for tail attack & I knew it was my job to hold them off. I pulled my flak suit off, threw my helmet off, turned on my trigger switch & was ready for what may come. They headed for Bruce & Pearson, flying off our wings before they hit us in numbers. Everything started to run thru my mind. Pilot said to be careful and take it easy. An FW came for me and I started shooting. Every attack but two were at 6:00 level and a dead-on shot. I let him have both guns and he started smoking & peeled beneath us. I looked up & saw Lt. Bruce's ship being attacked in formation by 7 fighters & at the same time, a fighter coming in at his waist. His guns were all firing away & at that split second, another fighter came in at his top side of fuselage. He was on fire and his plane got out of control. Another fighter started at his left waist and after throwing quite a bit of ammo, turned & headed for my tail, his engine already smoking. Fleming, left waist gunner, had hit him and now not knowing he was in trouble, he came in on me. I let go & after firing about 30 rounds, he blew up at about 50 yards away from my turret. He had it & Fleming & I were responsible for the kill. Lt. Bruce was completely in flames as I was later told by right waist gunner; no chutes emerged...His ship started toward us out of control, but French was on lookout for same. Another FW came in. I fired but he peeled off to our left.
